analogy.p: Imagine a strip of rubber with a team on each side, each person stretching their side. If more people stretch the shaded side, that side gets longer and the whole strip curves round towards the light, just as extra auxin makes shaded cells elongate so the shoot bends towards the light. The analogy breaks down for roots, where extra auxin slows growth on that side instead of speeding it up, and plants do not have people choosing to stretch: it is chemical signalling.
analogy.t: Auxin as extra stretching on one side of a rubber strip

bullets: A **hormone** is a chemical messenger that is made in one place, travels to a **target** tissue and brings about a change.
Plants make hormones in small amounts and they work at very low concentrations, just like animal hormones.
The three plant hormones in the AQA triple specification are **auxins**, **gibberellins** and **ethene**.
Plant hormones are triple (separate) science only: combined science students are not examined on them.
A plant that responds to a stimulus by growing is showing a **tropism**; the direction of growth is controlled by hormones, not by muscles.
Plant responses help the plant survive: reaching light for photosynthesis, anchoring roots in damp soil, and ripening fruit to spread seeds.
core.p: Plants have no nervous system, so they cannot use nerve impulses to coordinate their responses. Instead they use **plant hormones**, which are chemical messengers made in one part of the plant that move to another part and change how its cells behave. Plant hormones **control and coordinate growth** and allow plants to respond to their surroundings, especially to **light** and **gravity**. Because they are chemicals moving through tissues, plant responses are usually much slower than animal responses, which is why you can only see a plant bending after minutes or hours.

bullets: **Phototropism**: growth response to light. Shoots are **positively phototropic** (grow towards light).
**Gravitropism / geotropism**: growth response to gravity. Roots are **positively gravitropic** (grow down, with gravity); shoots are **negatively gravitropic** (grow up, away from gravity).
Roots are usually described as **negatively phototropic** (they grow away from light), though exam questions focus on the gravity response.
The stimulus must come from **one direction** to cause a tropism: light from directly above does not make a shoot bend.
Tropisms are slow growth movements, unlike reflexes, which are fast and use nerves.
Always name the organ: say 'the shoot is positively phototropic', not just 'the plant is positively phototropic'.
core.p: A **tropism** is a growth response of a plant to a directional stimulus. If the plant grows **towards** the stimulus the tropism is **positive**; if it grows **away** from it the tropism is **negative**. The two you must know are **phototropism** (response to light) and **gravitropism** (also called **geotropism**, the response to gravity). The word growth is important: a tropism is a change in the direction of growth, not a movement like a Venus flytrap snapping shut.

bullets: Auxin is made in the **shoot tip**; this is why removing the tip stops a shoot responding to light.
Auxin moves to the **elongation zone** just behind the tip where cells are lengthening.
In **shoots**: auxin stimulates cell elongation, so more auxin = more growth.
In **roots**: a high concentration of auxin **inhibits** cell elongation, so more auxin = less growth on that side.
The key idea is **unequal distribution of auxin**: if auxin is spread evenly the shoot grows straight; if it builds up on one side the organ bends.
Auxin does not make new cells; it makes existing cells **longer**, which is what changes the direction of growth.
Different parts of the plant respond to the same hormone in different ways because their cells have different sensitivities.
core.h: Auxin: where it is made and what it does
core.p: **Auxin** is the main plant hormone controlling tropisms. It is produced in the **tip of the shoot** (and root tips) and then moves back down the stem to the region behind the tip where cells are growing. In shoots, auxin **promotes cell elongation**: the cells get longer, and since cell elongation is how most plant growth happens, more auxin on one side means faster growth on that side. In roots the response is different, because a **high concentration of auxin inhibits cell elongation**.

bullets: Step 1: light shines on the shoot from **one side only**.
Step 2: auxin made in the tip is redistributed so that **more auxin collects on the shaded side**.
Step 3: auxin causes cells on the shaded side to **elongate faster**.
Step 4: the shaded side becomes longer than the lit side, so the shoot **bends towards the light**.
Step 5: once the tip points at the light, auxin is again spread evenly and the shoot grows **straight** towards it.
Common mark scheme phrase: 'auxin is unequally distributed, with a higher concentration on the shaded side, causing more cell elongation there'.
Survival value: more light absorbed means more photosynthesis, more glucose and faster growth.
core.p: When a shoot is lit from one side, auxin does not stay evenly spread. It moves across the shoot so that more auxin collects on the **shaded** side than on the lit side. This extra auxin makes the cells on the shaded side **elongate more** than the cells on the lit side. The shaded side therefore grows longer and the shoot **bends towards the light**. This benefits the plant because leaves in the light carry out more **photosynthesis**.

bullets: Stimulus: **gravity** acting on a horizontal shoot.
Auxin collects on the **lower side**.
Auxin **promotes** elongation in the shoot, so lower cells lengthen more than upper cells.
The shoot curves **upwards**: this is **negative gravitropism**.
Benefit: the shoot grows towards light and space above the soil, so leaves can photosynthesise.
Seen in real life when a plant is knocked over, or when a tree grows sideways out of a bank and then turns up.
core.p: If a shoot is placed on its side, gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the **lower side** of the shoot. Auxin stimulates elongation in shoots, so the lower side grows faster than the upper side. This makes the shoot curve **upwards**, away from gravity, a **negative gravitropic** response. The shoot keeps growing upwards until auxin is again evenly distributed.

bullets: Stimulus: gravity on a horizontal root.
Auxin again collects on the **lower side**.
In roots the extra auxin **inhibits** elongation, so the lower cells grow **less**.
Upper cells elongate more, so the root bends **downwards**: **positive gravitropism**.
Benefit: anchorage and access to **water and mineral ions** (for example nitrate, magnesium) in the soil.
Key comparison: **same hormone, same side, opposite effect** because shoot and root cells respond differently.
Examiners reward the idea that auxin has **different effects at different concentrations / in different tissues**.
core.p: In a horizontal root gravity also moves auxin to the **lower side**. But roots respond differently: a high concentration of auxin **inhibits** cell elongation. So the lower side of the root grows **more slowly** than the upper side, and the root bends **downwards**, in the direction of gravity. This is **positive gravitropism**. Roots growing downwards anchor the plant and reach water and mineral ions in the soil.

bullets: **Shoot**: auxin on lower side, growth **stimulated** on lower side, bends **up** (negative gravitropism).
**Root**: auxin on lower side, growth **inhibited** on lower side, bends **down** (positive gravitropism).
**Shoot** and light: positive phototropism; **root** and light: negative phototropism (usually).
In an exam, write both the **location** of the auxin and its **effect on elongation**.
Never say auxin 'makes the shoot grow towards light': say it makes cells on the **shaded side elongate**.
If a question gives a diagram of a seedling on its side, work out the lower side first, then apply the rule for that organ.
core.p: The easiest way to avoid mixing up the two gravitropism cases is to learn them side by side. In both organs auxin ends up on the lower side when the organ is horizontal. The difference is the effect that auxin has on cell growth. This is a classic exam question because it tests whether you can explain **why** the two organs bend in opposite directions rather than simply stating what happens.

bullets: Spec statement: gibberellins **initiate seed germination**.
Gibberellins can be used to **end seed dormancy**.
They can be used to **promote flowering**.
They can be used to **increase fruit size** (for example commercial seedless grapes).
Dormancy is a survival strategy: the seed waits until conditions (water, warmth, oxygen) are suitable for the seedling.
Growers can spray gibberellins on seeds or plants to control the **timing** of germination or flowering, giving crops ready at a chosen time.
Link: seed germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature as well as the hormone signal.
core.p: **Gibberellins** are plant hormones that **initiate seed germination**. Many seeds are **dormant**, which means they will not grow even if conditions seem good. Gibberellins end this dormancy, triggering the seed to begin germinating, so the seed grows only when conditions suit it. They also affect stem growth and flowering, which gives them uses in horticulture.

bullets: Spec statement: ethene **controls cell division and ripening of fruits**.
Ethene is a **gas**, so it can reach neighbouring fruit, not just the fruit that produced it.
Ripening changes: starch is converted to sugar, the fruit softens, the colour changes and the smell develops.
These changes make the fruit attractive to animals, which helps **seed dispersal**.
Unripe fruit is firmer, so it can be transported with **less damage** and longer shelf life.
On arrival, retailers can expose fruit to ethene to ripen it at the chosen time.
Storage: low temperatures and removing ethene from the store air can **delay** ripening.
core.p: **Ethene** is a plant hormone that is a **gas**. It controls **cell division** and **ripening of fruits**. As a gas it can spread through the air from one fruit to its neighbours, which is why one ripe fruit in a bowl speeds up the ripening of the others. In the food industry the use of ethene is controlled to manage when fruit ripens.

bullets: **Weedkillers**: synthetic auxins are sprayed on crops; **broad-leaved weeds** take up more and grow too fast, so they die, while narrow-leaved crops like cereals are mostly unaffected. This is a **selective** weedkiller.
**Rooting powder**: the cut end of a stem cutting is dipped in auxin so that it grows **roots** quickly, giving many new plants identical to the parent (**clones**).
**Tissue culture**: auxins promote growth of small groups of plant cells grown on a nutrient medium to make many identical plants.
**Ethene**: unripe fruit is picked, transported and stored, then ripened with ethene so that it arrives in good condition.
**Gibberellins**: end seed dormancy, promote flowering, increase fruit size.
Advantages: faster production, uniform crops, ripening at the right time, fewer losses in transport.
Possible issues: cost, and need for correct concentration, since too much hormone can harm plants.
core.h: Uses of plant hormones in agriculture and horticulture
core.p: Plant hormones are used commercially to control growth, saving time and increasing yield. The specification expects you to know specific uses of each hormone. Learn them as a list: **auxins**: weedkillers, rooting powders, tissue culture; **ethene**: fruit ripening in transport and storage; **gibberellins**: end seed dormancy, promote flowering, increase fruit size.

bullets: Independent variable: direction of the **light** or position (orientation) relative to **gravity**.
Dependent variable: the **direction / angle of bending** (measured with a protractor) or the **length** of growth on each side.
Control variables: type and age of seedling, temperature, water, light intensity (for the gravity test keep in the **dark** or evenly lit), and time.
Use a **control** seedling: for example one in uniform light or upright.
Use **several seedlings** and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of anomalies.
Gravity test: a **clinostat** (slowly rotating seedlings) removes the one-sided pull of gravity, so seedlings grow straight.
Safety: avoid hot lamps burning skin; wash hands after handling compost and cotton wool.
core.h: Investigating the effect of light or gravity on seedlings
core.p: The specification suggests investigating how light or gravity affects the growth of newly germinated seedlings. For light, seedlings are grown in a box with a small window cut in one side, or placed next to a lamp. For gravity, seedlings are germinated on damp cotton wool or agar in a container which is then turned onto its side. Careful control of other variables lets you decide that any bending is caused by the stimulus tested.

bullets: **Intact shoot** in one-sided light: bends towards light (normal response).
**Tip removed**: no bending, and little growth, because no auxin source.
**Tip covered with opaque foil cap**: grows straight up, because the tip cannot detect light so auxin is not redistributed.
**Base covered, tip exposed**: bends towards light, showing the **tip** is the sensitive part.
**Tip covered with transparent cap**: bends, because light still reaches the tip.
State the conclusion: the **tip** detects the light and produces auxin, which moves down to cause the bending.
Use the data: compare mean angle of curvature between conditions, not just general statements.
core.p: Classic experiments by Darwin and others used shoots with the tip removed, covered or the base covered to find which part detects light. Exam questions give results like these and ask for conclusions. Always link your answer to where **auxin** is made and where **light is detected**. The result is explained by whether auxin can be redistributed unevenly.

bullets: Both are **chemical messengers** that act on **target** cells at low concentration.
Plant hormones are made in **tissues** (like shoot tips), not in glands as in animals.
Animal hormones travel in the **blood**; plant hormones move through plant tissue (and ethene through the **air**).
Both give **slower, longer-lasting** effects compared with nerves.
Plant hormones control **growth direction**; animal hormones control many processes including metabolism and reproduction.
Same hormone, different effect depending on concentration or tissue is seen in both systems.
core.h: Plant hormones compared with animal hormones
core.p: Plant hormones share features with animal (endocrine) hormones but are not made in specialised glands. They are made in cells in particular regions such as shoot tips, and they move short distances by diffusion or through plant tissues rather than around the body in blood. Comparing the systems is a good way to see the general principle that hormones are chemical messengers with specific targets.

bullets: **Photosynthesis**: phototropism positions leaves for light.
**Transport in plants**: roots grow towards water and mineral ions taken up by active transport and osmosis.
**Asexual reproduction / cloning**: rooting powders and tissue culture produce clones.
**Adaptation and survival**: tropisms increase the chance of surviving and reproducing.
**Variables and investigations**: tropism experiments are common sources of 'plan an investigation' questions.
**Food security**: hormones help increase yield and reduce losses in the food supply chain.
core.p: Plant hormones connect to several other parts of the course. They explain how plants maximise photosynthesis, how crops are produced commercially, and they are an example of coordination and response without a nervous system. Use these links in extended answers.

exam: Command words: **state** (1 mark, name the hormone), **describe** (what happens), **explain** (needs because / reason, usually 2 to 4 marks).
For 'explain phototropism' (4 marks): shaded side, more auxin, more cell elongation, shoot bends towards light.
Always write **where** the auxin collects (shaded side / lower side) AND **what** it does to cell elongation.
Use the phrase **'unequal distribution of auxin'** in explanations.
For roots, include the word **inhibits**: 'high concentration of auxin inhibits cell elongation'.
For uses: give the hormone and the use, e.g. 'ethene is used to ripen fruit during transport and storage'.
Practical questions: name independent, dependent and control variables; use a mean of several seedlings; use a protractor to measure the angle.
For data: quote values (e.g. 'angle of 45 degrees compared with 0 degrees') and compare conditions.
Do not confuse tropisms (growth, slow, hormones) with reflexes (fast, nervous system).
A 6-mark question may ask you to compare shoot and root responses to gravity: structure as stimulus, auxin location, effect, direction, advantage.

mistakes.r: Auxin makes cells on the SHADED side elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.
mistakes.w: Auxin makes plants grow towards light.

mistakes.r: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, away from the light.
mistakes.w: Light makes auxin move to the light side.

mistakes.r: In shoots it promotes elongation, but a high concentration in roots inhibits elongation.
Auxin collects on the lower side and inhibits growth there, so the upper side grows more and the root bends down.
mistakes.w: Roots bend down because auxin makes the upper side grow.

mistakes.r: Auxin makes cells longer (elongation); it does not mainly cause cell division.
Ethene is a gas hormone that controls ripening and cell division.
mistakes.w: Ethene is a solid / liquid fertiliser.

mistakes.r: Ripening is ethene; gibberellins end seed dormancy, promote flowering and increase fruit size.
The shoot grows (changes direction of growth) towards the light; the plant itself does not move.
mistakes.w: The plant moves towards the light.

summary: AQA triple biology asks you to know that plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins and ethene) coordinate growth, to explain phototropism and gravitropism using unequal distribution of auxin, and to recall commercial uses of the hormones. It matters because tropism and hormone-use questions are standard 4 to 6 mark items requiring precise cause-and-effect explanations.

terms.d: A chemical messenger made in one part of a plant that moves to another part and affects growth or development.
A plant hormone made in the shoot tip that causes cell elongation in shoots and inhibits elongation in roots at high concentration.
A plant hormone that initiates seed germination, ends seed dormancy, promotes flowering and increases fruit size.
A gaseous plant hormone that controls cell division and the ripening of fruits.
A growth response of a plant to a directional stimulus.
The growth response of a plant to light from one direction.
The growth response of a plant to gravity.
The lengthening of plant cells, which is the main way plant shoots increase in length.
Auxin being at a higher concentration on one side of a shoot or root than the other.
A resting state in which a seed does not germinate even when conditions are suitable.
A herbicide that kills certain plants (such as broad-leaved weeds) but not the crop.
A powder containing auxin used to make stem cuttings grow roots.
Growing small pieces of plant tissue on a nutrient medium to produce new plants.
A genetically identical copy of an organism.

worked.ans: Auxin made in the tip builds up on the shaded side. It makes the shaded cells elongate more than the lit cells, so the shoot bends towards the light.
worked.q: Explain how a shoot grows towards light from one side. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: auxin is produced in the shoot tip.
Mark 2: auxin moves to / accumulates on the shaded side of the shoot.
Mark 3: auxin causes cells on the shaded side to elongate more.
Mark 4: the shaded side grows faster so the shoot bends towards the light.

worked.ans: The tip detects the light and produces the auxin that causes the elongation, so covering or removing it prevents the bending response.
worked.q: Seedlings were grown with light from the right. Seedling A: intact. B: tip covered with foil. C: tip removed. D: base covered with foil. A and D bent towards the light; B grew straight up; C did not grow. What do the results show about the tip? (3 marks)
steps: A and D bend, so the base is not needed to detect light.
B (tip covered) did not bend: the tip must detect the light.
C (tip removed) did not grow: the tip is the source of auxin needed for growth.

worked.ans: Auxin collects on the lower side and inhibits elongation there, so the upper side grows faster and the root curves down towards gravity.
worked.q: A seedling root is placed horizontally. Explain why the root grows downwards. (4 marks)
steps: Gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of the root.
A high concentration of auxin inhibits cell elongation in roots.
Cells on the upper side elongate more than those on the lower side.
